summary: Elmer Thomas opens by reframing AI as a tool to embrace rather than fear. Twilio's tiny Developer Education team faced three core pain points: error-prone first drafts from over 100 product teams, time-consuming grooming tasks (style checks, alt text, SEO), and hallucination risk from uncontrolled AI use. Rather than building one monolithic bot, they constructed six single-purpose agents behind a simple Next.js frontend. Each agent targets a repetitive, high-volume, low-creativity task: an automated editor for grammar and formatting, an image alt text generator for accessibility, a jargon simplifier translating developer-speak to plain English, an SEO metadata generator respecting character limits, a docs outline builder (still forthcoming) for navigation and structure, and a Slack-based triage bot for help-channel requests. The architecture routes requests through a Next.js UI into custom GPT models—specifically using the o1 model for the automated editor—with style guides and rubrics stored in Airtable for collaborative editing. A validation layer comprising Vail linting and CI/CD tests feeds into GitHub PRs with codeowner review, ensuring multiple human eyes before merging. Maria Bermudez then demos four agents live: the automated editor on a live URL, the SEO metadata generator, the alt text generator across multiple pages, and the jargon simplifier on prepared text. She notes the agents do not yet communicate with each other—a known limitation. Elmer returns to discuss guardrails addressing hallucinations (lint, CI tests, human reviewers), bias (dataset tests, prompt audits), and stakeholder misalignment (weekly or compressed PR reviews, Slack feedback loops). He closes with a three-step playbook: identify a throughput-killing pain, pick a repeatable rule-based task, and loop with users at least weekly to ship, measure, and refine.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Build multiple single-purpose agents rather than one monolithic bot; each agent should target a repeatable, high-volume, low-creativity task.
The o1 model was selected for the automated editor after experimentation, as it most consistently applies the team's style guide and rubric.
Style guides and rubrics are stored in Airtable so non-technical collaborators can easily contribute to prompt governance.
A layered validation pipeline—linting, CI/CD tests, GitHub PR codeowner review, and human merge—significantly reduces hallucination risk without slowing throughput.
Agents are not perfect; for example, the automated editor sometimes misses missing SEO descriptions, which a dedicated SEO metadata generator catches.
Guardrails extend beyond hallucinations to include bias mitigation (dataset tests, prompt audits) and stakeholder alignment (frequent PR reviews and Slack feedback loops).
A three-step playbook for adoption: identify a throughput-killing pain, pick a repeatable rule-based task, and loop with users at least weekly to ship, measure, and refine.
Agents currently operate independently and cannot yet communicate with each other—an acknowledged limitation requiring further work.

sections.title: Introduction and Reframing AI
sections.summary: Elmer Thomas introduces himself and the talk's tongue-in-cheek title, framing AI as something to embrace for working smarter. He outlines the agenda: pain points, agent architecture, a live demo by Maria Bermudez, and a stealable roadmap.

sections.title: Pain Points and Agent Overview
sections.summary: Elmer describes three headaches—error-prone first drafts from 100+ product teams, time-consuming grooming tasks, and hallucination risk—and introduces six single-purpose agents (automated editor, alt text generator, jargon simplifier, SEO metadata generator, docs outline builder forthcoming, Slack triage bot) behind a Next.js frontend.

sections.title: Architecture and Validation Flow
sections.summary: Elmer details the request flow: Next.js UI feeds a custom GPT model selected per job, with style guide and rubric retrieved from Airtable for collaboration. A validation layer includes Vail linting and CI/CD tests, GitHub PRs add codeowner review, and humans merge only when correct, significantly reducing hallucinations.

sections.title: Live Agent Demo by Maria Bermudez
sections.summary: Maria demonstrates four agents: the automated editor on a live URL using the o1 model with a diff view and rubric-linked explanations, the SEO metadata generator producing character-limited titles and descriptions, the alt text generator across multiple pages conforming to platform format, and the jargon simplifier producing a diff and revised text. She notes agents do not yet communicate with each other.

sections.title: Guardrails and Three-Step Playbook
sections.summary: Elmer returns to cover three guardrail categories: hallucinations (Vail Lint, CI tests, human reviewers), bias (dataset tests, prompt audits), and stakeholder misalignment (frequent PR reviews, Slack feedback loops enabling continuous prompt tuning). He shares a three-step playbook—identify a throughput-killing pain, pick a repeatable rule-based task, and loop with users weekly—and credits manager Carly Vanderwart and leadership.

demonstrations: Maria demos the automated editor by plugging in a live URL, showing a diff view with explanations of original text, revised text, and the relevant style guidance/rubric item.
Maria demos the SEO metadata generator by uploading a file and generating a meta title and meta description with character-limit awareness.
Maria demos the alt text generator by selecting multiple pages and generating alt text for all images, conforming to the docs platform's required format.
Maria demos the jargon simplifier by pasting prepared text and showing a diff editor plus a revised-text tab for quick copy into a PR comment or direct file edit.
limitations: The automated editor is not perfect—sometimes it catches a missing SEO description and sometimes it does not.
Agents currently cannot communicate with each other; making them talk to each other is future work.
Hallucinations are reduced significantly but not fully eliminated.
quantitativeClaims: Over 100 product teams submit first drafts to the small docs team.
Weekly PR review cadence, sometimes compressed to days or hours.
